supervisor.title: Let DSH bring itself back up?
supervisor.body: This hosted DSH instance is started by hand (or by something else) — when it dies it does not come back. I can install a supervisor of my own: it starts at login, it starts the host again when the process is gone, and it restores the last snapshot when the host does not come up. The supervisor never touches your session data; it only starts, watches and rolls back.
supervisor.changes: What it changes: a new <stateDir>/supervisor/ directory (the supervisor script, its configuration, its log and its lock); on Windows a login record (the scheduled task dsh-autorestart-web), on Linux a systemd user service. What it does NOT change: your session data, your model configuration, the installed plugins.
supervisor.rights: Which rights it needs: on Windows NO administrator rights (it runs "at login"; if the machine forbids ordinary users from creating scheduled tasks, it falls back to the startup folder, which needs none either); on Linux it needs write access to your own home directory (systemctl --user — an ordinary user is enough).
supervisor.uninstall: How to remove it: one click on "Start at login → Uninstall" in the settings; or by hand: schtasks /Delete /TN "dsh-autorestart-web" /F (on Linux: systemctl --user disable --now dsh-autorestart-web.service && rm ~/.config/systemd/user/dsh-autorestart-web.service). Both ways also delete the <stateDir>/supervisor/ directory.
supervisor.installHint: It writes a supervisor script into <stateDir>/supervisor/ and registers a login record on Windows / a systemd user service on Linux. No administrator rights needed. After that the host is started again within seconds when its process is gone; when it does not come up, the snapshot of the last restart is restored. You can uninstall it with one click at any time.
supervisor.keep: Keep the way I start it
supervisor.keepHint: Nothing is changed. Whatever starts the host today keeps starting it. The price: the host does not come back by itself when its process is gone — the restart only works while something else (a docker "restart: always", your own systemd unit) brings it back.
supervisor.laterHint: This card does not come back. You can install the supervisor by hand at any time in "Settings → Auto-restart & shut down → Start at login".

backup.section: What is backed up, and the manual backup steps
backup.recovery: A plugin will not start? Put that one back to its previous version
backup.label: Backup before a restart
backup.hint: Saved automatically before every restart, so a host that cannot boot again can be rolled back. What it holds: your settings (always); plugins you wrote yourself and linked to their source directory (their files are copied too); plugins installed from the internet (only which ones and which version are recorded, the files are not copied, reinstall them from that list if something goes wrong).

backup.evidenceHint: "Certified by" says WHY a copy counts as safe: all four startup checks passed, the health probe answered in command mode, it is the first-install seed, or a human confirmed a manual rollback. "Not certified" means there is no evidence at all — such a copy is never treated as a safe one. When a boot had to be rescued by the watchdog, the evidence records that too, so a later selector can refuse that copy.

fallback.seed: There is also a first-install seed copy (settings only, not verified, used only when the copy above is unavailable), {time}, {size}
fallback.other: There is also an unverified copy (never restored automatically, used only when the copy above is unavailable), {time}, {size}

backup.othersSummary: {n} more pre-restart snapshots (unverified, never restored automatically)
backup.identityHint: A backup has one of two identities: ① “known good” — the copy a boot has proven; when something breaks, only a known-good copy is rolled back, and the first install creates one automatically. ② “this restart's snapshot” — taken right before every restart and not proven yet; old backups (unverified) and that snapshot are never rolled back automatically. At most {n} copies are kept together (the oldest goes first; a known-good copy is never deleted). A manual rollback asks for confirmation first, then restarts automatically.
backup.rollbackConfirmBody: The backup from {time} will be restored over the current state — **what you have now is replaced** (a snapshot of it is taken first, so this rollback can be undone).
backup.rollbackConfirmRestart: A restart follows automatically; this page disconnects during it and works again afterwards.

backup.footprint: Using {size} on disk, {n} copies right now
backup.purpose: A complete backup of the local plugins, taken before every restart; at most {n} copies are kept, and you can roll back to any one you pick.
backup.kindsLocal: Both linked plugins (written by hand) and localized ones (their directory has a .git) are in the copy in full, so they can be rolled back.
backup.kindsThirdParty: Third-party plugins are maintained by their authors; if something is wrong, reinstall them.

watchdog.title: If a restart fails, it can rescue you automatically
watchdog.explain: This plugin ships with an automatic rescue: when a newly restarted version never comes up (about 3 minutes), it puts a verified working backup back and starts the program again, so you do not have to do it yourself. **It is on by default — it came with the plugin.** If it has no trusted backup, it will not guess: it tells you there is no trusted restore point and asks you to handle it manually. If it did anything, it leaves a record of what it tried and how it went.
watchdog.whereOff: If you do not want it, turn it off on the settings page — with it off, a new version that does not start has to be handled by hand.
watchdog.noticeSaved: That is the only notice; it will not appear again.
watchdog.warnOff: With it off, a new version that does not start has to be handled by hand.
watchdog.savedOn: The watchdog is on: the next restart is protected.
watchdog.savedOff: The watchdog is off: the next restart will not roll back on its own.
